paras: The attempted lynching of circus workers in Chesaning, Michigan, took place on June 8, 1881. A mob of about 300 townspeople tried to lynch four employees of a traveling circus who were held in connection with the killing of a village policeman. A posse of twelve men held the crowd back with revolvers and put the prisoners on a train to Saginaw City. Two of the four, Sim Robinson and William Murray, were described as "colored"; the case reached readers mainly through Chicago Tribune dispatches and Michigan state-news columns.

Late on the night of June 6, after a performance of Hilliard & DeMott's circus, a group of men attached to the show attacked a crowd at a bowery dance in the village, according to dispatches from East Saginaw. Special policeman Augustus Emery was beaten to death, Fred Wenzel was reported fatally injured, and village president J. B. Griswold was knocked down and badly bruised. Charles Homer was shot in the face, reportedly while helping to quell the riot. The Paw Paw True Northerner wrote that "the circus men appear to have been the aggressors."

Thirteen men were arrested in all: eight were jailed at Saginaw City on June 7, four were held at Chesaning, and one was arrested near Lansing. Early wire reports said that five men had been arrested and that "with difficulty the people were restrained from lynching them." The Chicago Tribune's East Saginaw correspondent wrote on June 7 that the four held at Chesaning would likely "be taken out and hanged to-night," because excitement in the village was at "fever heat."

On June 8, according to the Tribune's correspondent, a crowd tried to lynch four circus employees "implicated in the murder of Monday night": J. Hughes, John Quinn, Sim Robinson and William Murray. A posse of twelve escorted them to the depot and kept "the mob of fully 300 men" back with loaded revolvers. The prisoners were put on the train and taken to Saginaw City, where all were to appear in court the next day. The dispatch identified Robinson and Murray as "colored" and said Murray came from Chicago.

No report of the court hearing, an inquest verdict on Emery's death or a trial was found in the coverage, and no paper reported that anyone was lynched. A post-mortem examination of Emery's body found two blows to the left temple and one that fractured the skull.

The story reached distant readers mainly as a wire account of the affray, printed under headlines such as "Serious Melee," "Murderous Roughs" and "A Bloody Circus Row" in Wheeling, Sacramento and Los Angeles. The longer version, with its line that the people were restrained from lynching, kept running in weekly news summaries in Wisconsin, Minnesota and Michigan as late as June 17. These reports cast the circus men as "roughs" and "desperados" and treated the townspeople's anger as understandable.

Only the Chicago Tribune printed the June 8 attempt itself, as a short special headed "Attempted Lynching" among other crime items. It neither praised nor condemned the mob, described the prisoners as "implicated in the murder," and gave the race of only the two Black men. In Michigan, the Cheboygan Northern Tribune reprinted a Post and Tribune dispatch that singled out "a negro" among the rioters as the one who "may be lynched."

The accounts differ on what happened to the prisoners at Chesaning. The Tribune's dated special from East Saginaw says the posse kept the mob back and sent all four to Saginaw City. The undated Post and Tribune summary says the Chesaning people had got possession of one Black rioter and does not mention the train, so it may describe an earlier moment. Reported arrest counts range from five to thirteen, and one Grayling item gives the date of the affray as June 7 rather than June 6.

reader.title: Attempted lynching of circus workers in Chesaning, Michigan
bases: A mob of about 300 tried to lynch four circus employees held for a killing and was held off by a posse of twelve (A5); earlier dispatches said the prisoners would likely be 'taken out and hanged' (A2) and that the people were 'restrained from lynching them' (A1).

A crowd of 'fully 300' sought to lynch prisoners accused in a policeman's death, a group acting without legal authority on a pretext of justice, but no one was killed: the posse put the prisoners on a train to Saginaw City (A5; A2). No report of a later lynching appears in the coverage.

The Chicago Tribune's own East Saginaw correspondent (A2, A5), the press-association wire (A1, A2) and a Post and Tribune dispatch (A10) independently report crowds at Chesaning seeking to lynch the prisoners, though only A5 describes the June 8 scene at the depot.

accounts.label: Chicago Tribune East Saginaw correspondent
accounts.gist: On June 7 the correspondent wrote that four men held in the Chesaning jail would likely be taken out and hanged that night. On June 8 he reported that a mob of 300 had tried to lynch four prisoners and was held off at the depot by a posse of twelve, which put the prisoners on a train to Saginaw City.

accounts.label: Western Associated Press wire
accounts.gist: The wire reported that five of the gang were arrested and that the people were restrained 'with difficulty' from lynching them, and that thirteen arrests were made in all.

accounts.label: Post and Tribune dispatch (via Northern Tribune)
accounts.gist: According to this dispatch, four prisoners were in the Chesaning lock-up and 'the Chesaning people' had got possession of one rioter, 'a negro', who 'may be lynched'.

framing.detail: The Chicago Tribune ran the attempt as a short item headed 'ATTEMPTED LYNCHING' among other crime dispatches. It praised neither the mob nor the posse, but said the prisoners were 'implicated in the murder' and noted that two were 'colored'.

Papers from California to Minnesota ran the affray under headlines such as 'Murderous Roughs', 'A Bloody Circus Row' and 'Serious Melee', treating the circus men as aggressors; several added that the people were restrained from lynching them.

Michigan weeklies treated it as state news. The Northern Tribune singled out 'a negro' who 'may be lynched' without comment, and the Paw Paw True Northerner noted that one prisoner was a local man's son.

record_check.dossier: Accused of a role in the killing of special policeman Augustus Emery during an attack by circus employees on a bowery dance on the night of June 6.

The mob threatened the prisoners at the depot and was held back by armed guards. No seizure is reported in A5, though A10 says the townspeople got possession of one Black prisoner. The record should say threat or attempt, not siege.
Townspeople of Chesaning ('the Chesaning people'); a mob of about 300, none named.
Four reports carry the lynching threat or attempt (A1, A2, A5, A10), and the wire line on the people being restrained from lynching was reprinted into mid-June.

info: The lynching attempt took place on June 8, 1881 ('to-day' in a June 8 dispatch); the attack at the dance that led to it took place late on Monday night, June 6.
Chesaning, Michigan; the prisoners were escorted to the depot and put on a train to Saginaw City.
Four employees of the circus: J. Hughes, John Quinn, Sim Robinson and William Murray. Robinson and Murray were described as 'colored', and Murray was said to be from Chicago.
They were accused of a role in the killing of policeman Augustus Emery during an attack by members of Hilliard & DeMott's circus on a bowery dance.
The papers name no one in the mob. A Post and Tribune dispatch credited 'the Chesaning people'.
The prisoners were brought by train to Saginaw City and were to be brought into court on June 9; no later report of the court hearing was found.
